# Introduction (2.5 Pages)

<!-- Plastic Problem -->
Plastics is a societal paradox and a climate decision [@macreadie2025].
More than 450 million tonnes of plastics are produced annually [@dokl2024] for applications across sectors such as healthcare [@leissner2019], construction [@kamaruddin2017], automotive [@ravina2023], and particularly in the packaging industry [@tamizhdurai2024]. 
At the same time, the environmental impact of the linear model of mass production and consumption makes plastic waste a part of the chemical pollution in the planetary boundaries [@oneill2018;@biermann2020], putting in danger the safe operating limits of humanity [@villarrubia-gomez2024].
In the EU, the packaging sector is the largest contributor to plastic flows, both in terms of consumption and waste generation.
In 2019, approximately 14.5 Mt of plastic were used for packaging, accounting for 33% of total plastic consumption, while 14.1 Mt of packaging waste were generated, representing 49% of total post-consumer plastic waste [@amadei2023]. 
Only 38% of the 28.8 Mt of total post-consumer plastic waste generated was separately collected, while approximately 13% was mismanaged [@amadei2023]. 
Likewise Latin America represents roughly the 4% of global plastics production, about 14.4 Mt in 2018 of which 40% were used for the packaging sector. However, since the region is not a large productor, most of this plastics production remains in local consumption [@Brooks2020].

Indeed, the accumulation of microplastics in natural environments [@laskar2019; @thompson2024a] and  the long-term environmental effects of plastic waste remain poorly understood, as plastics do not readily re-enter established biogeochemical cycles [@gontard2022].
<!-- Centralized approach Problem -->
Therefore, around 60% of plastic production ends up in landfills or the environment, contributing to negative environmental externality ecological risks, including those associated with marine plastic pollution in the form of plastic litter [@suhaimi2022; @taylor2026; @zhang2025].
Plastic waste management has traditionally been designed around economies of scale and centralized waste-management systems.
However, these limitations reveals a wicked problem that goes beyond waste management alternatives [@lerpiniere2025].


Although a contested concept [@kirchherr; @corvellec2021;@giampietro2022;@rodl2022a], the notion of circular econmoy concept (CE) has taken political impulse in EU [@rizos2025] and Latin America as a vital framework for rethinking production and consumption patterns. 
The CE seeks to decouple economic growth from resource consumption by promoting strategies such as reduction, reuse, recycling, and redesign of materials and products [@villarrubia-gomez2026; @villarrubia-gomez2026; @figge2023]. 
Within the context of plastics, this approach emphasizes the need to close material loops and extend the lifecycle of resources across the entire value chain [@shamsuddoha2024; @schirmeister2022].
The transition to CE requires more than just improved waste management. 
It demands a systemic transformation involving all stakeholders to eliminate inefficiencies and capture lost value. 
Analyzing the plastics value chain (from raw material extraction to production, distribution, consumption, and end-of-life management) reveals multiple points where inefficiencies and value losses occurs. 
Addressing these inefficiencies requires not only improvements in waste management systems but also systemic transformations involving product design, innovation, and stakeholder coordination. 
Despite growing global awareness and a robust move toward these kinds of models, recycling rates remain stubbornly low, and many innovative solutions developed within academic ecosystems fail to reach industrial scale (Castelo-Vinueza, 2025).
Therefore, a value chain perspective is essential to identify opportunities for circularity and to implement effective interventions (Johansen et al., 2022).

From an enterprise adoption perspective, transitioning toward circular manufacturing requires understanding how manufacturing companies integrate circular strategies across micro (product and firm level), meso (supply chain and industrial symbiosis), and macro (regional) scales. At the micro level, physical implementation of 3R strategies (reuse, remanufacture, recycle) and cleaner production depend heavily on circular design decisions made at the beginning of the product lifecycle to enable end-of-life material recovery [@Dagiliene2020]. Furthermore, applying neo-institutional theory reveals that enterprise adoption and environmental reporting of circular practices are strongly driven by normative pressures, industry standards, and peer legitimacy rather than strict coercive legislative mandates alone [@Hoof2025]. This theoretical lens helps explain why firms frequently institutionalize corporate sustainability policies to secure social legitimacy and market access, even when their internal R&D structures and technological innovation capabilities remain underdeveloped [@Hoof2025]. In Latin America, enterprise adoption faces distinct operational barriers, including resource scarcity, high capital requirements for machinery modernization, low technical absorptive capacity in small enterprises, and market distortions caused by informal supply chains and volatile recycled material prices [@Gallego-Schmid2025; @Ujiyama2027].

To address these persistent operational bottlenecks, recent literature emphasizes a critical implementation gap in CE strategies [@rodriguez-meza2025]. While 10-R typologies provide broad policy direction (refuse, rethink, reduce, reuse, repair, refurbish, remanufacture, repurpose, recycle, recover), global circularity rates remain low because environmental targets are rarely translated into sector-specific engineering frameworks [@rodriguez-meza2025]. In Latin America, government CE plans exhibit a pronounced "silo approach", heavily concentrating policy instruments on end-of-life waste management while under-prioritizing eco-design and green manufacturing. Product design remains the least addressed phase in regional government plans, despite determining up to 80% of a product's lifecycle impact. Furthermore, recycled plastic markets across Latin America remain underdeveloped due to low investment in decontamination technologies, uncoordinated collection networks, and severe market price volatility [@Silva2021].

While technology transfer (TT) and CE transitions have been extensively investigated in the Global North, empirical research detailing the specific dynamics, mechanisms, and institutional obstacles within Latin America and specifically Colombia remains poor [@Gallego-Schmid2025, @ujiyama2027]. Specifically, existing literature lacks empirical characterization regarding how macroeconomic and structural environment barriers intersect with organizational maturity across enterprise scales.  Furthermore, there is a knowledge gap regarding operational strategies for university-industry alignment. Specifically, how Technology Transfer Offices (TTO) can be reconfigured as flexible boundary units and how university capabilities and multi-stakeholder co-creation strategies can de-risk industrial adoption within emerging regional markets [@Silva2021].

From a TT perspective, executing effective knowledge flows requires understanding the interaction between transferors, transferees, transfer objects, channels, and demand environments [@bradlow2024]. In green industrial restructuring, global technology transfer is essential to prevent developing nations from remaining trapped at low value-added segments of global value chains [@tsai2026]. Within circular supply chains, technology transfer is governed by qn qbsorptive capacity, requiring organizations to overcome institutional inertia, sense market shifts, and dynamically reconfigure operational routines to integrate post-consumer or bio-based materials [@lee2024]. In university-industry collaborations (UICs) marked by goal ambiguity, knowledge exchange relies on relational governance, which is mainly built upon trust, shared language, and networks, or a hybrid of formal contracts and relational mechanisms [@ollila2025]. Furthermore, academic and industrial practitioners crossing organizational boundaries undergo in-between identity workss to reconcile conflicting institutional logics [@abusaa2025], while university structural social capital serves as an intermediary platform for cross-industry knowledge sharing [@Lau2020].

<!-- Problem -->
While technology transfer and circular economy transitions have been extensively investigated in the Global North, empirical research detailing the specific dynamics, mechanisms, and institutional obstacles within Latin America and specifically Colombia remains poor. 
Specifically, existing literature lacks empirical characterization regarding how macroeconomic and structural environment barriers intersect with organizational maturity across enterprise scales. 
<!-- Knowledge Gap -->
Furthermore, there is a knowledge gap regarding operational strategies for university-industry alignment. 
Specifically, how Technology Transfer Offices can be reconfigured as flexible boundary units and how university capabilities and multi-stakeholder co-creation strategies can de-risk industrial adoption within emerging regional markets.

This study identifies that the transition is hindered by deep-seated economic and structural barriers. 
For instance, post-consumer recycled (PCR) material is frequently more expensive than virgin resin, and the country lacks a sufficiently integrated collection and sorting infrastructure, especially in remote regions (Lau et al., 2020; OECD, 2022). 
Furthermore, a climate of mutual distrust complicates the relationship between academia and industry; companies often perceive academic research as "utopian" or too theoretical for daily operational needs, while academics are frequently obstructed by rigid institutional bureaucracy and complex intellectual property rules. 
Consequently, many technological advancements in sustainable materials and waste valorization remain confined to laboratory prototypes and academic publications rather than becoming viable industrial solutions (Grafström & Aasma, 2021; Rosenboom et al., 2022).
The main purpose of this paper is to identify the institutional and organizational barriers that hinder effective technology transfer practices between academy and the colombian plastic value chain.
and to propose alignment strategies that bridge the gap between academic capabilities and industrial needs in the Colombian plastics sector. 
The research utilizes mixed-methods approach across four distinct phases: a documentary analysis of national regulations, a productive sector diagnosis involving 92 companies, an analysis of the Universidad Nacional’s technical capabilities, and the co-creation of strategies through international workshops. This study provides essential, evidence-based insights to support the development of a more resilient, sustainable, and competitive industrial model in Colombia.



# Background Literature (3 Pages)

  ## CE of plastics in Latin America


Some key aspects of CE in plastics value chains include innovative technologies, regulatory frameworks, and strategic practices that enhance recycling and reduce reliance on virgin materials [46, 47]. Emerging technologies such as chemical recycling, additive manufacturing, and microwave-assisted pyrolysis are pivotal in enhancing the circularity of plastics [48, 49]. Additionally, the integration of digital technologies facilitates better tracking and management of plastic waste, improving recycling rates and efficiency [50]. 

Within the aims of these CE models, extended producer responsibility (EPR) forces producers to manage the lifecycle of their products, incentivizing eco-design and sustainable practices [51]. National regulations aim to reduce plastic incineration and promote recycling, which is crucial for achieving circularity [52]. Additionally, implementing industrial symbiosis can improve the recycling efficiency of plastic waste, creating a more integrated value chain [53, 54](Neves et al., 2019; Marinelli et al., 2021). Emphasizing strategies such as reducing, reusing, and recycling can significantly improve the sustainability of plastic manufacturing processes [52]. Though CE presents a promising framework for addressing plastic waste, some challenges remain in technology adoption, regulatory compliance, and the need for systemic changes across the entire value chain [55, 56]. 

In Latin America and the Caribbean, the transition toward a circular economy operates under structural conditions that differ substantially from those in the Global North [32, 35]. Although the region accounts for approximately 4% of global plastic resin production (~14.4 million tonnes annually), over 40% of this production is absorbed by short-life packaging applications. Because Latin America is not a primary resin exporter, the vast majority of locally manufactured or imported plastic remains within domistic municipal waste streams, exacerbating local environmental externalities and ocean plastic leakage [57, 58]. The legislative architecture across Latin American nations has made notable strides, exemplified in Colombia by CONPES 3874 of 2016 for solid waste management, CONPES 4011 of 2020 for sustainable entrepreneurship, CONPES 4069 of 2021 for science and technology, Resolution 1407 of 2018 establishing Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) for packaging, Law 2232 of 2022 mandating the gradual phase-out of single-use plastics, Law 2277 of 2022 enacting a national single-use packaging tax, and Resolution 0803 of 2024 linked to recycled content traceability standards (NTC 6632) [59-65].

However, comparative evaluations of national circular economy plans across different Latin American countries reveal focus on global trends [66]. Government plans concentrate policy instruments predominantly on end-of-life waste collection and formalization of informal waste pickers, while systematically under-prioritizing eco-design, feedstock substitution, and financial support for circular technology R&D [33, 67]. Product design remains the least addressed phase in regional policy portfolios, despite determining up to 80% of a product's lifecycle environmental impact [66, 68]. Furthermore, recycled plastic markets across Latin America remain fragmented due to low capital investment in decontamination technologies, uncoordinated municipal collection networks, and severe market price volatility [69, 70].

At the regional level, the political momentum surrounding the CE for plastics has materialized through national strategies, roadmaps, and municipal policy instruments across several Latin American and Caribbean nations. Comprehensive assessments of regional governance indicate that countries such as Chile, Uruguay, Ecuador, Colombia, Costa Rica, and Peru have established formal national frameworks aimed at transitioning away from linear petrochemical reliance [66]. For instance, in Peru, the National Circular Economy Roadmap to 2030 prioritizes sustainable industrial production, eco-labeling, single-use plastic restrictions, and target-driven funding for research, development, and innovation through public-technical interfaces [58]. Similarly, Uruguay’s national circular action plans demonstrate how smaller South American economies leverage public-private partnerships, research centers, and waste recovery schemes to stimulate new circular markets for secondary polymers [68]. At the urban scale, city-level frameworks such as Bogotá’s Circular Economy Strategy (2023–2040) act as critical localized testing grounds where subnational governance models translate national directives into operational waste sorting, industrial symbiosis networks, and multi-actor waste management protocols [67]. Together, these national and municipal developments demonstrate a growing regional commitment to institutionalizing circularity within Latin America’s urban and industrial governance architectures.

Despite these legislative advancements, significant structural gaps and value chain imbalances persist throughout Latin America’s circular transition. Regional evaluations reveal that most government initiatives remain heavily concentrated on end-of-life waste collection and resource recovery models, while giving insufficient attention to upstream circular product design, microplastic regulation, and the elimination of hazardous chemical additives. Furthermore, national plans often address plastic pollution in isolation, missing crucial strategic linkages to broader climate change mitigation and biodiversity conservation goals [66]. From an economic and social perspective, circular business models across LAC cities and nations encounter severe market frictions, including volatile prices for recycled resins, limited capital investment for advanced decontamination infrastructure, and the ongoing social marginalization of informal waste pickers. Overcoming these bottlenecks requires moving beyond semi-circular waste management toward holistic value chain frameworks that pair targeted financial incentives and public RDI funding with technical assistance for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) and formal labor integration for grassroots recycling networks [58, 68].

  ## TT within CE policies

Technology Transfer (TT) serves as a core mechanism for green industrial restructuring, enabling the bidirectional flow of scientific knowledge, technical know-how, and physical equipment from research institutions to the productive sector [71, 72]. In global value chains, effective technology transfer is essential to prevent developing economies from remaining trapped in low value-added, resource-extractive activities [37]. Organizations must overcome institutional inertia, sense emerging regulatory standards and market shifts, and dynamically reconfigure operational routines to integrate post-consumer or bio-based resins.

Within the Triple Helix framework connecting academia, industry, and government, university-industry collaborations (UICs) marked by goal ambiguity and novel scientific research face significant alignment challenges [73, 74]. Classical technology transfer models focused strictly on patent commercialization and transactional licensing often fail in multi-stakeholder sustainability transitions [36, 75]. Instead, knowledge exchange relies heavily on relational governance whichh is built upon mutual trust, shared technical language, and collaborative networks, or a hybrid mix of formal contracts and relational mechanisms [75]. Furthermore, university structural social capital acts as an intermediary platform for cross-industry knowledge sharing [41], while individuals acting as boundary spanners perform 'in-between identity work' to reduce academic and commercial logics [40].

To overcome institutional inertia and operational bottlenecks in circular transitions, recent scholarship highlights the necessity of multi-actor governance architectures, particularly government-led Triple Helix frameworks integrating university R&D, industrial capabilities, and state policy [76]. Within emerging and developing economies, where public funds and R&D infrastructure are chronically limited, Public-private partnerships act as vital catalysts for both circular economy implementation and digital transformation, bridging capital gaps and technical uncertainties across complex supply chains [77]. At the corporate level, large manufacturing and multinational firms overcome systemic barriers in plastic packaging by deploying integrated organizational strategies, combining eco-design mandates, cross-sectoral collaborative alliances, and institutional enablers that facilitate sustainable raw material substitution [78]. When aligned, these public-private and academic-industrial integration mechanisms establish the institutional scaffolding required to move circular policies from high-level legislative intent to operational manufacturing realities [76].

Beyond institutional governance, driving circularity across plastic supply chains requires integrating industrial symbiosis, economic market incentives, and digital technologies. Industrial symbiosis serves as a primary operational strategy for sustainable development, allowing transforming firms to exchange plastic waste streams as secondary industrial feedstocks through inter-firm networks and shared infrastructure [79]. However, the commercial viability of secondary polymers remains highly sensitive to market pricing; quantitative competition modeling shows that economic incentive policies (such as targeted secondary material subsidies and virgin resin taxation) are indispensable for bridging the price disparity between virgin and recycled plastics [80]. In resource-constrained and developing regions, these economic mechanisms are increasingly supported by digital enabling environments, such as IoT tracking, mobile reporting apps, and decentralized digital platformes which overcome supply chain fragmentation, enhance post-consumer material traceability, and foster inclusive stakeholder engagement across both formal and informal plastic waste ecosystems [81].

  ## CE adoption in small enterprises

Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) constitute a significant part of of manufacturing establishments in Latin America's plastics subsector (particularly over 98.5% in Colombia) [82]. Consequently, the success of regional circular economy policies hinges upon the capacity of small enterprises to adopt sustainable product designs, process optimizations, and material recovery practices [30, 83]. Manufacturing firms adopt Circular Manufacturing (CM) strategies across three scales: micro (product and single firm level), meso (inter-firm networks and industrial symbiosis), and macro (regional and national systems) [30]. At the micro level, implementing physical 3R strategies (reduce, reuse, recycle) requires integrating eco-design choices from the initial stages of product conceptualization [45].

However, applying neo-institutional theory demonstrates that corporate adoption and environmental reporting are strongly driven by normative pressures, industry standards, and peer legitimacoes rather than strict legislative enforcement alone [31]. This explains why firms frequently establish corporate sustainability policies to secure social legitimacy, even when their internal R&D structures remain underdeveloped. Resource constraints severely differentiate MSME circular transitions from those of large multinational corporations [23]. Small companies operate under tight cash flow constraints, relying on legacy machinery that is technically unsuited for processing PCR materials. They lack dedicated internal R&D departments, specialized technological management personnel, and financial reserves to absorb the commercial risks of eco-design re-engineering [82]..s

At an international level, the literature highlights diverse operational frameworks, adaptation strategies, and business model innovations aimed at enabling SMEs to adopt CE principles. The international adaptation mechanisms, demonstrate how government tax incentives, advisory programs, and digital technologies such as Product-as-a-Service models, reverse logistics, and artificial intelligence facilitate the transition of SMEs away from traditional linear paradigms [84]. Focusing on the plastics sector, Jürgens et al. present a low-threshold lifecycle framework for SMEs, showing through Life Cycle Assessments (LCA) that while bio-based feedstocks and post-industrial recyclates offer environmental benefits, achieving truly closed-loop material cycles requires product-specific recovery systems and supportive local infrastructure [85]. However significant barriers for circular plastics start-ups including high capital intensity, investor skepticism, and low market credibility, show how start-ups deploy key success factors such as circular value proposition design, market sensitivity, networking prowess, and circular ambidexterity to survive, though many remain constrained to incremental recycling rather than radical waste hierarchy shifts [86]. Complementing these aspects, categorize SME circularity barriers across macro, meso, and micro levels, help to propose practical mitigation strategies such as participating in public R&D grants to offset initial capital costs, expanding supplier networks to mitigate seasonal input risks, and implementing internal organizational training [87].

In emerging and developing economies, the adoption of circular business models faces distinct behavioral, financial, and institutional hurdles that require localized diagnostic and policy approaches. In countries such as Nigeria endogenous there’s a relationship between perceived plastic waste mismanagement risk and firm-level effectiveness, where high anticipated adaptation costs and constrained loan access lead managers to favor low-investment, locally sourced packaging solutions over complex supply chain overhauls [88]. Although, some circular business models in Mexico and Colombia, show that despite advancing legal frameworks, widespread implementation is constrained by expensive commercial credit (where only 44% of Colombian SMEs apply for loans due to cost), regulatory ambiguities between authorities, inadequate regional recycling infrastructure, and persistent consumer price sensitivity [89, 90].
